claims.text: The lightweight high-entropy alloy can combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
A stable, refined grain structure contributes to the stated combination of properties.
A homogeneous distribution of elements enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Thermomechanical processing by hot isostatic pressing or forging followed by controlled cooling modifies grain size, grain morphology, and elemental distribution.
The proposed processing window is 800–1000 °C, a strain rate of 10^-3–10^-1 s^-1, and a cooling rate of 1–10 °C/min.
The alloy's elemental distribution produces solid-solution strengthening.
Formation of a protective oxide layer contributes to corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Thermomechanical processing will improve mechanical strength relative to the baseline alloy.
Thermomechanical processing will improve corrosion resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
Thermomechanical processing will improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the baseline alloy.
The baseline is a conventional low-entropy alloy with a similar nominal composition.
The hypothesis should cease to hold when processing temperature exceeds 1200 °C.
The hypothesis should cease to hold when cooling is faster than 100 °C/min.
Processing above the proposed boundaries causes elemental inhomogeneity or undesirable phase formation.
The exact relationship among processing conditions, grain structure, and mechanical properties is not well established.
The roles of precipitates and defects are not fully understood.
